headline: Yellowfin and early white marlin light up the eastern wall as the Gulf Stream eddy pinches Veatch and Hydrographer
subhead: A warm-water push against the canyon rims has yellowfin stacked on the color, bigeye working the night chunk slick, and the first real white marlin bite of the summer showing at Oceanographer.
body_markdown:
Last week gave us a decent window and I took it. Wind sat out of the southwest most days, building an afternoon sea breeze that made the run home lumpy but left the mornings flat enough to fish the troll properly. That matters more than people think — a clean morning means you can actually read the color change instead of fighting a washing-machine chop trying to find it. The moon's working through toward first quarter right now, which means the tide swing offshore is moderate, not the big springs we get around new and full. Out here that mostly shows up in how tight the eddy pinches against the canyon wall — with a softer tide push this week, the warm water has stayed pinned in against the 100-fathom curve instead of sloshing back and forth, and that's been good news for anybody running out to Veatch or Hydrographer.

What's coming this week is more of the same setup, maybe better. Water's still warming — the blue push along the eastern wall has been holding in the mid-to-upper 70s where it shoulders up against the green, and that boundary is exactly where the bite has concentrated. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't turn hard onshore, that eddy should stay locked against the rim through the weekend, which is the whole ballgame for a one-day run from Montauk. If it swings northeast, the warm water gets pushed off the edge and I'd rather stay dockside than burn fuel chasing a moving target.

Atlantis has been the most consistent of the four this past week. I ran to the 60-fathom break around 39°48'N, 71°02'W Tuesday and again Thursday, and both days the temp break was holding tight right on the edge where it drops into the canyon proper. Yellowfin in the 50-70 pound class have been eating a naked ballyhoo behind a green machine or a small Ilander/ballyhoo combo pulled at 6-7 knots, spreader bar in the shotgun position doing the real work drawing them up. Not a bonanza — I'll be honest, Tuesday we had three bites and boated two, Thursday it was five for three — but that's a respectable eastern canyon day in mid-July, and the fish have been quality, not rats.

Veatch has been the sleeper. The eddy's been sitting up on the north wall around 40°02'N, 69°24'W, and that's put a nice push of 74-degree water right up against the structure in 50 to 100 fathoms. We chunked butterfish there Wednesday afternoon into evening and connected on bigeye after dark — 120 and 140-pound class fish, both on a straight butterfly chunk with a glow stick clipped above a circle hook, baits sent back 15-20 feet under the slick with no added weight. That's a night program, not a day trip, so plan your fuel and your crew rotation accordingly if you're running from Block Island — it's roughly 90 miles out, so you're committing to an overnight unless you've got the range and the patience to run home in the dark.

Hydrographer has been quieter but not dead. The color change there has been less defined than at Veatch, more of a soft gradient than a hard rip, and the yellowfin bite reflected that — scattered, a few singles on the troll around 39°52'N, 69°00'W, nothing like the pods we found at Atlantis. Mahi have been mixed in wherever we found floating debris or lobster gear balls, nothing huge, mostly 8-15 pounders, but good eating and they'll hit a small bucktail tipped with a strip of squid or a chunk of butterfish if you cast to them instead of trolling past.

The real story this week, though, is Oceanographer, where we finally saw the first legitimate white marlin action of the season. Squid have been building around the eastern grounds — the same push that's supercharged the Rhode Island and Nantucket rips inshore has spread offshore too, and where there's squid stacked on the temp break, the billfish show up behind them. We had four white marlin bites Friday working the edge around 39°58'N, 68°08'W, converting two on ballyhoo pulled flat and dropped back on circle hooks after the fish showed on the long teasers. That's early for a big number, but it's the kind of sign that tells you the pattern's starting, not finished.

Fuel math on that run from a Rhode Island port — Point Judith out to Oceanographer is a solid 110-plus miles each way, which means you're burning the better part of your tank just getting there and back before you fish a drop of fuel on the grounds. I don't make that run unless the forecast is clean both days and the intel's fresh, because there's no cutting that trip short if the weather turns.

Looking ahead: if this southwest wind pattern holds and the eddy stays pinned against the wall like it has been, I'd put my money on Atlantis for the most reliable yellowfin troll bite and Veatch for the night chunk program on bigeye. Oceanographer's white marlin bite is the one I'm watching closest — two fish off four bites isn't a trend yet, but if the squid stay stacked out there through this week, that number should build. Either way, check the wind before you check anything else. A clean run out is worth more than any bait choice you'll make once you're on the grounds.
